title: Cranberry juice may slow plaque and acid on teeth

caption:
Cranberry juice has a reputation for being sour, acidic and sugary, the opposite of what your dentist wants. A new study suggests the pure stuff might actually help your teeth.

Researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry tested it on 22 people: 14 children and 8 adults. Each person swished one of three drinks: pure, unsweetened 100% cranberry juice, a cranberry juice cocktail with added sugar, or plain water. The team then compared plaque samples taken before and 30 minutes after.

The result: plaque exposed to the pure cranberry juice grew back more slowly, and it produced less acid, in both kids and adults. Acid from plaque bacteria is what wears down teeth and leads to cavities.

"Most people think of cranberry juice as very sour, very acidic and sugary, and therefore may not contribute positively to oral health," said lead researcher Christine Wu, a professor of pediatric dentistry. "This study found the opposite."

Before you stock up, there's a big catch. It's a small study, and it only measured what happened in the 30 minutes after swishing, so it can't say whether drinking cranberry juice regularly actually prevents cavities. Larger, longer studies are needed. And the benefit was seen with pure, unsweetened juice, which is intensely tart. Wu suggests a sugar substitute could make it easier to drink.

Source: University of Illinois Chicago via ScienceDaily; study published in Scientific Reports
